notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material from Enduring Word (Guzik), Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Barnes, Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB), Matthew Henry and the NET Bible notes. I found nothing for some areas, so they are left out:
- **Protestant disagreements:** none of the pages I read showed the traditions taking different sides on any verse of this chapter. Where commentators differ, it is over how to translate the Hebrew, not over theology.
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I read none.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching:** I found none on this chapter.

I couldn't open Gill's full chapter page, so his notes below come only from search excerpts.

---

**v. 1:** Guzik sees a cruel irony here: the sons of men Job wouldn't have put with his sheepdogs now mock him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/ — Barnes says respect for the aged was a top virtue in that culture, so being mocked by the young cut deep. These men were valued below Job's dogs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/30-1.htm — Gill says the mockers are not the three friends. They were older men of good standing. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/30-1.html — Matthew Henry says the fathers were too untrustworthy for even the lowest job, minding the sheep. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_030.cfm

**v. 2:** Ellicott says this verse describes the fathers, and verses 3 and following describe their children. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-30.html — Barnes says their strength wasn't worth noticing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html — The NET notes read the rare Hebrew word as "strength" and see no reason to change the text. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 3:** JFB, following older translations, prefers "gnawers of the wilderness." It says Job is describing the roughest desert tribes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/jfb/job/job_030.cfm — Barnes agrees they lived by gnawing roots and shrubs. He links the word to "gnawing pains" in v. 17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html

**v. 4:** The Pulpit Commentary says the plant is not really mallow but probably a salty desert shrub. The "juniper" is a kind of broom with a very bitter root, eaten only when people were desperate. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-30.html — Barnes agrees only the very poorest would eat it. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsv/job/30-4.html — Gill compares them with the prodigal son craving pig food. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/30-1.html

**v. 5:** JFB says that when these drifters raided villages they were chased off like thieves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-30.html — The Pulpit Commentary says outcast tribes, pushed onto barren land, almost always turn to robbery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/30.htm — Matthew Henry is harsher: he blames laziness and says people who won't work for their bread are in effect stealing. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_030.cfm

**v. 6:** The Pulpit Commentary points to rocky country like the area around Petra. The Greeks called such cave-dwellers "Troglodytes." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/30-6.html — Barnes says the word means frightening, remote valleys. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html

**v. 7:** The NET notes say the verb means "to bray," a sign of an animal's hunger. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print — JFB says "huddled" literally means "poured out." It pictures them sprawled here and there behind the thorn bushes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-30.html

**v. 8:** Barnes says "nameless" means men of no reputation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html — Guzik quotes Smick: Job describes them six ways not to gloat but to show how deep his own disgrace is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/

**v. 9:** Ellicott says the cross-references make a Messianic reading of Job's complaints fitting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-30.html — JFB sees a close parallel with the mockery Jesus suffered. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_030.cfm

**v. 10:** The Pulpit Commentary links the spitting with how the crowd treated Christ, and says Job's sufferings pictured Christ's. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-30.html — Barnes says even this low-born group now keeps its distance from Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html

**v. 11:** This is a known textual question. The written Hebrew text says "his cord"; the reading marked in the margin says "my cord." The NET notes give three possible meanings:
- "my tent cord," as in 29:20;
- "my bowstring," meaning Job has been disabled;
- "his cord," meaning God has stopped holding back.

https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=job&chapter=30&verse=11

JFB prefers "his cord." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_030.cfm — The Pulpit Commentary says "He" can only be God, who has taken away Job's strength. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/30.htm — Matthew Henry gives both readings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_030.cfm

**v. 12:** Barnes says the right hand is the place of honour, which makes the insult worse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html — The NET notes say the Hebrew word for "rabble" appears only here and comes from a root meaning "young bird." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 13:** The Pulpit Commentary takes "no one to restrain them" as "they dare this without powerful backers." It notes the text may be damaged; the Latin Vulgate reads "there is none to help me." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/30.htm — The NET notes mention Gordis's suggestion "they put thorns in my path." Most take it to mean they ruin Job's way of escape. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 14:** Guzik quotes Smick: Job pictures himself as a city with a broken wall, with siege machines rolling through the rubble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/ — The Pulpit Commentary pictures water bursting through a dam, wave after wave. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/job-29.html

**v. 15:** The Pulpit Commentary links the "terrors" with Job's nightmares (7:14) and the "terrors of God" (6:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/30.htm — Barnes says the word for "dignity" suggests Job's generous, noble spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html

**v. 16:** Guzik says this was first of all a crisis of the soul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/ — The NET notes say it can mean Job is wasting away or that he is grieving. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 17:** The Pulpit Commentary matches the night-time bone pain to a form of elephantiasis. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/30.htm — The NET notes say the one doing the piercing could be the night or God. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 18:** Ellicott lists two readings: God's power has disfigured "the garment of my skin," or Job's clothes stick to his sores. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-30.html — The NET notes point out that tunics didn't have collars, so "neck" fits better. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 19:** Ellicott says "dust and ashes" appears only three times in Scripture: here, Job 42:6 and Genesis 18:27. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-30.html — The Pulpit Commentary says "the mire" is the lowest depth of misery. Barnes says God is the one throwing Job down. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/30-19.html

**v. 20:** The Pulpit Commentary says feeling forsaken by God is the worst of all calamities, and compares Jesus' cry from the cross. It adds that no good man is ever truly forsaken: Job should have trusted more and complained less. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/30.htm — Guzik quotes Lawson: like us, Job wrongly takes God's silence as displeasure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/ — The NET notes say the switch from talking about God to talking to God shows strong emotion. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 21:** Guzik quotes Morgan: Job really did charge God with cruelty, and his protest was nearing revolt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/ — The Pulpit Commentary calls Job's view of God as his enemy a "fearful perversion" of the truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/job-30.html

**v. 22:** Ellicott offers a second reading that contrasts Job's past and present: God once lifted him onto the wind, and now dissolves him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-30.html — The NET notes say the written text reads "storm." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 23:** Guzik notes that Job was sure he would die soon, but he recovered and got back double. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/ — The Pulpit Commentary says Job was right that everyone dies, but wrong that his own death was about to happen. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-30.html — Barnes links "appointed" with Hebrews 9:27. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html

**v. 24:** Ellicott calls the verse "hopelessly uncertain." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-30.html — JFB reads it as Job's faith about life after death. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_030.cfm — Matthew Henry reads it as the grave bringing quiet. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_030.cfm — Guzik reads it as an appeal: God would not strike a heap of ruins that cries out to Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/

**v. 25:** Guzik quotes Spurgeon: a minister who cannot feel should resign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-30/ — Matthew Henry says those who helped the poor will find comfort in remembering it when they are sick. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_030.cfm

**v. 26:** Ellicott contrasts this with 3:25–26: there Job expected the worst; here he hoped for good and was let down. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-30.html — The Pulpit Commentary says the "light" may mean hoped-for breaks in his suffering that never came. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/30.htm

**v. 27:** The NET notes say the Hebrew is literally "my bowels boil," which can be taken as inner turmoil or as literal. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=30&mode=print

**v. 28:** Ellicott prefers "I go mourning without the sun" over "blackened." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-30.html — Barnes contrasts this with the past: Job once stood up in the assembly to give advice, and now stands up to weep. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/job-30.html — Constable thinks v. 28 is about Job's emotions and v. 30 about his body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/30-19.html

**v. 29:** The NET notes say Job's cries sound like these animals' howls. It doesn't mean he lives with them. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Job+30%3A29%2C30 — The Pulpit Commentary mentions the jackals' long cries at night. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/30.htm

**v. 30:** Guzik lists darkened, peeling skin and fever among Job's symptoms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/ — The NET notes say "bones" means the whole body and the heat is fever. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Job+30%3A29%2C30

**v. 31:** JFB says these instruments belong to times of joy, which makes using them for grief sadder. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_030.cfm — In its homiletic section, the Pulpit Commentary says the harp still plays, unlike the harps hung up in Psalm 137, but now in sad notes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/job-30.html

---

**Notes on traditions:**
- **Christ-centred reading.** JFB, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary read the mockery and spitting (vv. 9–10) as pointing to Christ. They agree with each other; this isn't a split between traditions.
- **Commentators' traditions.** Studylight's verse page lists Ellicott as Anglican and Barnes as Presbyterian, and tags the Geneva notes as Calvinist. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/30-19.html
